did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with a musical heading—“For the director of music: To the Lilies”—and also includes the attribution “of Asaph.”
The psalmist addresses the LORD using two central images: as a shepherd who leads Israel and as the One enthroned above the cherubim, asking Him to appear and reveal Himself.
Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh are mentioned together in the appeal. The psalmist asks the LORD to awaken His might and come to save His people.
The request “Restore us, God; let Your face shine on us, and we will be saved” serves as a refrain in the psalm, with slight variations in its wording each time.
The distress is described vividly in terms of weeping: the people eat “bread of tears” and drink tears in great measure, meaning an abundance of tears.
The people are described as having become an object of contention to their neighbors, meaning a target of dispute or conflict, while their enemies mock them.
Beginning with this verse, Israel is compared to a vine: the LORD brought it out of Egypt, drove out the nations before it, and planted it.
The description of the vine emphasizes its growth: it took root deeply and filled the land.
The vine’s branches are described as spreading to the sea and its shoots as reaching to the river, highlighting its size and extensive spread.
After describing the vine’s destruction, the psalmist asks the LORD to look down from heaven, take care of the vine, and tend it.

The psalmist asks that the LORD’s hand be upon “the man at Your right hand” and “the son of man” whom He made strong for Himself, linking the request for protection and strength with the restoration of life.
The psalm ends by repeating the request for salvation: the LORD God of Hosts is asked to restore His people, let His face shine on them, and save them.
